quote: Die Diophantische lineare Gleichung $ap+bq+c=0$ in Primzahlen $p, q$, lösen.
english: Solve the linear Diophantine equation ap+bq+c=0 in prime numbers p, q.
topic: Notes on solving linear Diophantine equations in primes (including twin primes), a plan to treat this via Weierstrass's theory of elementary factors and the Riemann–Roch theorem, primes among the values of a polynomial, remarks on the nature of mathematics, and a sketch of a proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra.

triage.modern_statement: Take fixed integers a, b, c that satisfy the natural coprimality and congruence conditions. Does the equation ax + by + c = 0 have a solution in primes x, y, and in the main cases infinitely many solutions? Two famous special cases are a=1, b=-1, c=±2, which is the twin prime conjecture (p − q = 2 infinitely often), and a=b=1, c=−N with N even, which is the binary Goldbach conjecture. In general this is the question of how often a two-variable linear form takes prime values at prime arguments.
triage.answered_by: Nobody has solved it. Hilbert published this question as part of his 8th Problem (Paris ICM, 1900). The diary note is evidently a private early version of that question. Partial results are known. For example, the work on bounded gaps between primes (Zhang, Maynard, Polymath) shows that some shift c ≤ 246 gives infinitely many solutions of p − q = c. But neither the twin prime case nor the Goldbach case has been proved, and neither has the general statement.

evidence.claim: Hilbert's 8th Problem (1900) asks, word for word, whether the linear Diophantine equation ax+by+c=0 (with given integral coefficients each prime to the others) is always solvable in prime numbers x and y. He presents it as a generalisation of Goldbach's problem and the twin prime problem.

Wikipedia lists the solvability of two-variable linear Diophantine equations in primes as one part of Hilbert's 8th problem. It says the twin prime and Goldbach conjectures are special cases and that very few particular results toward a solution exist.
Wikipedia also says the lower bound for prime gaps shows that some c ≤ 246 makes the equation (p − q = c) have infinitely many prime solutions. This is a partial result only.
Research papers still treat the problem as open and propose related conjectures, for example that ax+by=n is solvable in primes for every n ≥ (a−1)(b−1).

triage.why: The note's wording, ap+bq+c=0 in primes p and q, matches the text of Hilbert's 8th Problem almost exactly. The page also mentions twin primes, which Hilbert names there as a special case. The problem includes the twin prime and Goldbach conjectures, both still unproved, so it remains open. Work on it is active, notably on bounded prime gaps and on the Goldbach problem. Claimed full proofs found online, such as the arXiv paper math/0701235 by Jinzhu Han, have not been accepted by mathematicians. One gap in the sources: the specific prime-gap researchers (Zhang, Maynard, Polymath) are named from general background, not from the search results; the sources only state the c ≤ 246 result.
